[notes-n1] Notes 1. Retaining walls: what they do and how they fail
A retaining wall holds soil at a steeper face than the soil would keep by itself, wherever the ground level changes abruptly: a road in cutting, a basement, a platform on a slope. The soil it holds pushes on it sideways. The wall must send that push into the ground without turning over, sliding or overloading the ground, and each of its parts must carry its bending and shear. This Unit takes the stability; Unit 14 takes the parts.
[Figure: The three stability failures: overturning about the toe, sliding on the base, and bearing failure under the toe (course notes: overturn, slide, settle).]
The course notes list three ways a wall fails the ground. It overturns when the moment of the thrust about the toe exceeds the moment of the weights. It slides when the thrust exceeds the friction under the base. It settles , or fails in bearing, when the pressure under the toe exceeds what the ground can carry. The three checks use the same table of loads; they differ in the partial factors and in what they compare.
[Figure: Types of wall. A gravity wall relies on its own weight; a cantilever wall on the weight of the backfill standing on its heel; counterforts and buttresses brace the stem of a high wall.]
Type How it stands Typical use
Gravity its own weight; plain concrete or masonry, the thrust line kept in the middle third so that no tension develops low walls, to about 3 m
Cantilever a vertical cantilever (stem) on a wide base slab; the weight of the soil on the heel does most of the holding economical to about 8 m
Counterfort stem and base tied together at intervals by bracing walls behind the stem, in tension high walls, above 6 to 7 m
Buttress the same, with the bracing in front, in compression where the space in front can be given up
The notes also name gabion, crib, tieback and segmental (keystone) walls, which hold soil by other means. This course designs the cantilever wall in full (Units 13 and 14); the RC Design app adds a gravity wall, a counterfort wall and a basement wall for comparison.
[Figure: The parts of a cantilever wall and the first dimensions of the course notes and Mosley. The thrust is taken on the virtual back, over the whole height H.]
A cantilever wall has a stem , which holds the soil, and a base slab with a toe in front of the stem and a heel behind it. First dimensions come from experience: a base of 0.6H to 0.7H, a stem about 80 mm thick at its root for every metre of backfill, tapering to about 0.6 of that at the top, a base as thick as the stem root, and a toe about twice that thickness. For the 4.5 m stem of the notes’ wall this gives a 400 mm stem root, 240 mm at the top, a 400 mm base 3.2 m wide and an 800 mm toe. These are a first trial; the three checks decide the base.
Quick check (not graded): A cantilever wall is 4.9 m high from the top of the backfill to the underside of its base. By the first-dimension rule, its base is about
Options: 1.5 to 2.0 m wide | 2.9 to 3.4 m wide | 4.9 m wide | 0.4 m wide
Explanation shown after answering: B = 0.6H to 0.7H = 2.94 to 3.43 m; the notes take 3.2 m. 0.4 m is the thickness of the stem root (80 mm per metre of the 4.5 m of backfill, rounded up).
Key points:
- Three stability failures: overturning about the toe, sliding on the base, bearing under the toe.
- Gravity walls stand by their own weight; cantilever walls by the soil on the heel; counterforts and buttresses brace high walls.
- First trial: B = 0.6H to 0.7H; stem root 80 mm per metre of backfill; base as thick as the stem root; toe about twice that.

[notes-n2] Notes 2. Active pressure and the two thrusts
Soil is not a liquid: it has shearing strength, so it pushes sideways with only a fraction of its vertical pressure. When the wall yields a little, the soil behind it relaxes to its smallest sideways pressure, the active pressure. Rankine’s theory gives that fraction, K_a, from the angle of shearing resistance φ alone.
EQUATION (13.1): K_a = \frac{1-\sin\varphi}{1+\sin\varphi}
For the well-drained sand of the notes’ wall, φ = 35° and K_a = (1 − 0.574)/(1 + 0.574) = 0.271. At a depth z below a level surface the vertical pressure is γz, plus any uniform surcharge w that stands on the backfill (traffic, stored material, a slab on grade). The pressure on the wall is K_a times that:
EQUATION (13.2): p = K_a\,(\gamma z + w)
[Figure: The active pressure of Worked Example 13.1: γ = 19 kN/m³, φ = 35°, w = 10 kN/m², H = 4.9 m.]
The diagram has two parts. The soil gives a triangle, zero at the surface and K_aγH at the bottom; its resultant acts at a third of the height. The surcharge gives a rectangle, K_aw at every depth; its resultant acts at mid-height. Per metre length of wall:
EQUATION (13.3): P_s = \tfrac{1}{2}K_a\,\gamma\,H^2 \ \ \text{at } \frac{H}{3}, \qquad P_q = K_a\,w\,H \ \ \text{at } \frac{H}{2}
For the notes’ wall, P_s = ½ × 0.271 × 19 × 4.9² = 61.8 kN/m at 1.63 m above the underside of the base, and P_q = 0.271 × 10 × 4.9 = 13.3 kN/m at 2.45 m. The soil thrust is a permanent action; the surcharge thrust is a variable one. They are kept apart in every step that follows, because they take different partial factors.
Which height? For stability the wall and the soil on its heel move together as one body. The thrust is therefore taken on the virtual back , the vertical plane through the end of the heel, from the surface down to the underside of the base: H = h_3 + h = 4.5 + 0.4 = 4.9 m, not the 4.5 m of the stem. Stopping at the top of the base loses 16 % of the soil thrust here (52.1 instead of 61.8 kN/m) and is the commonest slip in this topic. The stem alone is loaded over 4.5 m; that is for its bending in Unit 14.
Three conditions stand behind these formulas: the backfill is level, it is granular (c = 0, as in the notes), and it is drained. Water behind a wall adds its full pressure, 9.81 kN/m² for every metre of depth against about 5 kN/m² for this sand, and lifts the base as well; weep holes and a drainage layer behind the stem keep it away. A sloping backfill and a water table come in Unit 14.
Quick check (not graded): γ = 19 kN/m³, φ = 35°, w = 10 kN/m², H = 4.9 m. The total characteristic thrust on the virtual back, P_s + P_q, is
Options: 61.8 kN/m | 75.1 kN/m | 64.3 kN/m | 136.9 kN/m
Explanation shown after answering: 61.8 + 13.3 = 75.1 kN/m. 61.8 leaves out the surcharge; 64.3 uses the stem height of 4.5 m; 136.9 forgets the ½ of the triangle.
Quick check (not graded): A uniform surcharge w on the backfill adds, on the wall,
Options: a pressure K_aw, the same at every depth | a triangle of pressure, like the soil | nothing: it acts downward only | a point load at the top of the stem
Explanation shown after answering: The surcharge raises the vertical pressure by w at every depth, so the sideways pressure rises by K_aw everywhere: a rectangle, with its resultant K_awH at mid-height. It also loads the heel, w per metre, which matters in §3.
Key points:
- K_a = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ); p = K_a(γz + w).
- Soil: triangle, P_s = ½K_aγH² at H/3 (permanent). Surcharge: rectangle, P_q = K_awH at H/2 (variable).
- H runs from the surface to the underside of the base, on the virtual back through the heel end.
- Level, granular, drained backfill; water and slopes in Unit 14.

[notes-n3] Notes 3. The table of loads and moments about the toe
Every stability check starts from one table: each load on a metre length of wall, its lever arm about the toe A, and its moment. Build the table once, with characteristic values and no factors; the three checks then pick from its sums.
[Figure: The loads of Worked Example 13.1 and their moments about the toe A, per metre length of wall.]
The vertical loads are weights: the stem, split into a triangle and a rectangle when it tapers, the base, and the soil standing on the heel (concrete 25 kN/m³, the soil at its own γ). Each acts at its centroid; the arm is measured from A, the end of the toe, because that is the point the wall would turn about. The horizontal loads are the two thrusts of §2, with arms H/3 and H/2 measured up from the underside of the base. Moments of the weights turn the wall back onto its heel: they are restoring . Moments of the thrusts turn it over the toe: they are overturning .
Load kN/m Arm about A (m) Moment (kN m/m) Kind
W_1 stem, tapered part: ½ × 0.16 × 4.5 × 25 9.0 0.8 + ⅔ × 0.16 = 0.907 8.2 permanent, restoring
W_2 stem, rectangle: 0.24 × 4.5 × 25 27.0 0.8 + 0.16 + 0.12 = 1.08 29.2 permanent, restoring
W_3 base: 0.4 × 3.2 × 25 32.0 1.60 51.2 permanent, restoring
W_4 soil on the heel: 19 × 4.5 × 2.0 171.0 0.8 + 0.4 + 1.0 = 2.20 376.2 permanent, restoring
W_q surcharge on the heel: 10 × 2.0 20.0 2.20 44.0 variable, restoring
P_s soil thrust 61.8 4.9/3 = 1.633 101.0 permanent, overturning
P_q surcharge thrust 13.3 4.9/2 = 2.45 32.5 variable, overturning
Four sums come out of the table, and they are all the checks need. Permanent, vertical: ΣV_{k,G} = 239.0 kN with ΣM_{r,G} = 464.7 kN m. Variable, vertical: V_{k,Q} = 20.0 kN with M_{r,Q} = 44.0 kN m. Permanent, horizontal: H_{k,G} = 61.8 kN with M_{o,G} = 101.0 kN m. Variable, horizontal: H_{k,Q} = 13.3 kN with M_{o,Q} = 32.5 kN m. Note where the weight comes from: the soil on the heel is 171 of the 239 kN. The concrete of the whole wall is only 68 kN.
The surcharge appears twice The same surcharge pushes the wall over (its thrust, 13.3 kN) and holds it down (its weight on the heel, 20 kN). The two effects are listed apart, because the stability checks treat them in opposite ways: the thrust is an unfavourable variable action and is always counted; the weight on the heel is a favourable variable action, and a favourable variable action is taken as zero (§4). The surcharge might be standing only beyond the heel.
Two things are left out on purpose. The soil in front of the wall could resist sliding by its passive pressure, but it is often dug out or backfilled loosely later, so the course ignores it, as the notes and Mosley do. The soil over the toe is ignored as well. Both omissions are on the safe side.
Quick check (not graded): In the notes’ wall (toe 0.8 m, stem 0.4 m, heel 2.0 m), the lever arm about A of the soil standing on the heel is
Options: 1.0 m | 1.6 m | 2.2 m | 3.2 m
Explanation shown after answering: The soil block is 2.0 m wide and starts 1.2 m from A: 0.8 + 0.4 + 2.0/2 = 2.2 m. 1.6 m is the centre of the base; 3.2 m is the heel end, where the vertical part of a sloping thrust would act (Unit 14).
Key points:
- One table per metre of wall: load, arm about the toe A, moment; characteristic values.
- Keep four sums: permanent and variable, vertical (restoring) and horizontal (overturning).
- The surcharge is listed twice: its thrust (unfavourable) and its weight on the heel (favourable).
- Passive resistance in front and the soil over the toe are ignored.

[notes-n4] Notes 4. Overturning and sliding
A wall is unstable when a large push meets a small weight. So the stability checks do the opposite of what a column design does: they factor the push up and the weight down. The rule behind every number in this section is one question, asked of each load in each check: does it help or does it harm?
Check Weights (permanent, help) Soil thrust (permanent, harms) Surcharge thrust (variable, harms) Surcharge on the heel (variable, helps)
Overturning (EQU) 0.9 1.1 1.5 0
Sliding, combination 1 1.0 1.35 1.5 0
Sliding, EC7 Combination 2 1.0 1.0, with K_{a,d} 1.3, with K_{a,d} 0
Overturning is a check of static equilibrium (EQU): moments about the toe A. The overturning moments take 1.1 (permanent) and 1.5 (variable); the restoring moment of the weights takes 0.9; the surcharge on the heel takes nothing.
EQUATION (13.4): 1.1\,M_{o,G} + 1.5\,M_{o,Q} \ \le\ 0.9\,M_{r,G}
For the notes’ wall: 1.1 × 101.0 + 1.5 × 32.5 = 159.9 kN m against 0.9 × 464.7 = 418.2 kN m. The wall is 2.6 times safe against overturning; a wall whose base satisfies the other checks nearly always is.
Sliding is resisted by friction under the base: μ times the vertical load, where μ = tan δ is the coefficient of friction between the concrete and the ground. In combination 1 the thrusts take 1.35 and 1.5 and the weights 1.0:
EQUATION (13.5): 1.35\,H_{k,G} + 1.5\,H_{k,Q} \ \le\ \mu\,\left(1.0\,V_{k,G}\right)
For the notes’ wall: 1.35 × 61.8 + 1.5 × 13.3 = 103.4 kN against 0.5 × 239.0 = 119.5 kN. The check passes with 16 % to spare, and the course notes stop here. Sliding is usually the check that decides the base, as Mosley observes.
[Figure: The same wall in the two sliding checks. Combination 1 factors the loads; Combination 2 factors the strength of the soil.]
Why a second combination? Eurocode 7 (MS EN 1997-1, Design Approach 1) asks for two combinations, and the design must satisfy both. Combination 1 puts the uncertainty on the loads: 1.35 and 1.5 on the actions, the soil at its characteristic strength. Combination 2 puts it on the ground: the actions take 1.0 and 1.3, and the strength of the soil is divided by 1.25, as tan φ. A weaker soil pushes harder (K_a rises) and grips less (μ falls), so both sides of the sliding check move the wrong way. The course notes and Mosley’s sliding check use the load factors only; the RC Design app checks both combinations, and so does this course.
EQUATION (13.6): \varphi_d = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\tan\varphi}{1.25}\right), \qquad K_{a,d} = \frac{1-\sin\varphi_d}{1+\sin\varphi_d}
EQUATION (13.7): \left(1.0\,H_{k,G} + 1.3\,H_{k,Q}\right)\frac{K_{a,d}}{K_a} \ \le\ \frac{\mu}{1.25}\,V_{k,G}
For the notes’ wall: φ_d = tan⁻¹(tan 35°/1.25) = 29.26°, K_{a,d} = 0.343, so every thrust grows by K_{a,d}/K_a = 1.267. The sliding force is (61.8 + 1.3 × 13.3) × 1.267 = 100.2 kN; the friction is (0.5/1.25) × 239.0 = 95.6 kN. The wall slides, by 5 %. Lengthening the heel from 2.0 to 2.2 m adds 19.1 kN of weight and brings the friction to 103.2 kN (Worked Example 13.1).
Where friction is not enough and the base cannot grow, a key under the base (a heel beam) adds the passive resistance of the ground in front of it; that is Unit 14.
Quick check (not graded): In the sliding check of combination 1, the weight of the soil on the heel is multiplied by
Options: 1.35 | 1.0 | 0.9 | 0
Explanation shown after answering: The weight helps the wall to resist sliding: a favourable permanent action takes 1.0 here. 0.9 is its factor in the overturning (EQU) check; 1.35 would overstate the friction by a third, on the unsafe side; 0 is for a favourable variable action, such as the surcharge on the heel.
Quick check (not graded): EC7 Combination 2 for a sand with φ = 35°: the design angle φ_d = tan⁻¹(tan φ/1.25) is
Options: 28.0° | 29.3° | 35.0° | 43.8°
Explanation shown after answering: tan 35° = 0.700; 0.700/1.25 = 0.560; tan⁻¹ 0.560 = 29.3°. The factor divides tan φ, not φ: 35/1.25 = 28.0° is the slip. With 29.3°, K_{a,d} = 0.343 against K_a = 0.271.
Key points:
- Overturning (EQU): 1.1M_{o,G} + 1.5M_{o,Q} ≤ 0.9M_{r,G}.
- Sliding, combination 1: 1.35H_{k,G} + 1.5H_{k,Q} ≤ μ × 1.0V_{k,G}.
- Sliding, EC7 Combination 2: φ_d = tan⁻¹(tan φ/1.25); thrusts × 1.0 and 1.3 with K_{a,d}; friction (μ/1.25)V_{k,G}.
- A favourable variable action counts as zero: leave the surcharge on the heel out of every resistance.
- Passive resistance in front of the base is ignored.

[notes-n5] Notes 5. The resultant, the middle third and the bearing pressure
The base of a wall is a strip footing under an eccentric load: all the vertical load, pushed towards the toe by the moment of the thrust. Unit 10’s pressure formula applies as it stands. The only new step is finding where the resultant meets the base.
The course checks the bearing pressure with characteristic (service) loads against the allowable bearing pressure q_a, as the notes do. Here every load counts, the surcharge on the heel included: N_k = ΣV_{k,G} + V_{k,Q}, and the net moment about the toe is ΔM_k = the restoring moments less the overturning moments. The resultant meets the base at x from A, and its eccentricity is measured from the centre of the base:
EQUATION (13.8): \bar{x} = \frac{\Delta M_k}{N_k}, \qquad e = \frac{B}{2} - \bar{x} \ \le\ \frac{B}{6}
For the notes’ wall: N_k = 239.0 + 20.0 = 259.0 kN; ΔM_k = 464.72 + 44.0 − 100.96 − 32.53 = 375.23 kN m; x = 375.23/259.0 = 1.4488 m; e = 1.6 − 1.4488 = 0.1512 m, well inside B/6 = 0.533 m. Inside the middle third the whole base stays in contact and the pressure is a trapezium:
EQUATION (13.9): q_{max},\ q_{min} = \frac{N_k}{B} \pm \frac{6\,N_k\,e}{B^2}, \qquad q_{max} \ \le\ q_a
Here q = 259.0/3.2 ± 6 × 259.0 × 0.1512/3.2² = 80.94 ± 22.95, that is 103.9 kN/m² at the toe and 58.0 kN/m² at the heel end, against q_a = 200 kN/m². The bearing check passes easily; on weaker ground it is the toe pressure that sizes the base (Faded Example 13.2).
[Figure: The resultant inside the middle third gives a trapezium; outside it part of the base lifts and the pressure becomes a triangle.]
If e exceeds B/6, the heel end lifts, because soil cannot pull. The pressure becomes a triangle whose centroid lies under the resultant, so the contact length is 3 x and
EQUATION (13.10): q_{max} = \frac{2\,N_k}{3\,\bar{x}} \qquad \text{(}e \gt B/6\text{: contact over } 3\bar{x}\text{)}
A lifting heel loses friction where it lifts and rocks the wall under changing loads, so the course does not accept it under service loads: when e > B/6, widen the base, usually at the toe.
The toe pressure at the ultimate limit state Mosley (§10.8.2) also finds the toe pressure under the factored loads, and the RC Design app does it for every wall: combination 1 (thrusts × 1.35 and 1.5), combination 2 (× 1.0 and 1.3) and EC7 Combination 2. In combination 1 each weight takes 1.35 if it raises the toe pressure and 1.0 if it lowers it. A vertical load at x from the toe changes the toe pressure by (W/B)(4 − 6x/B), so it raises it when its centroid lies within 2B/3 of the toe: the wall’s own weight usually does, the soil on the heel usually does not. For the notes’ wall the three values are 146.5, 110.4 and 132.8 kN/m², all below 200. The app compares them with q_a, which is an allowable (service) value: that is on the safe side, and a failure there is marked for review rather than as a certain failure of the wall. In hand calculations the service check above is the course check.
Quick check (not graded): A wall on a 3.0 m base has N_k = 240 kN and a net moment about the toe of 300 kN m. The resultant is
Options: inside the middle third: e = 0.25 m ≤ 0.50 m | outside it: e = 1.25 m | at the centre: e = 0 | outside it: e = 0.75 m
Explanation shown after answering: x = 300/240 = 1.25 m from the toe; e = 3.0/2 − 1.25 = 0.25 m; B/6 = 0.50 m. 1.25 m is x , measured from the toe, not the eccentricity, which is measured from the centre.
Quick check (not graded): The same wall (B = 3.0 m, N_k = 240 kN, e = 0.25 m). The pressure at the toe is
Options: 80 kN/m² | 100 kN/m² | 120 kN/m² | 40 kN/m²
Explanation shown after answering: N/B = 80; 6Ne/B² = 6 × 240 × 0.25/9 = 40; q_{max} = 80 + 40 = 120 kN/m² at the toe and 40 kN/m² at the heel end.
Key points:
- Service loads, all of them: N_k = ΣV_{k,G} + V_{k,Q}; ΔM_k = restoring − overturning, about the toe.
- x = ΔM_k/N_k from the toe; e = B/2 − x ≤ B/6 (the middle third).
- q = N_k/B ± 6N_ke/B²; q_{max} at the toe ≤ q_a.
- Outside the middle third: q_{max} = 2N_k/3 x over a contact of 3 x ; the course asks for a wider base.
- The app also reports the toe pressure at the ULS, compared with q_a on the safe side.

[notes-n6] Notes 6. Sizing the base: the heel holds, the toe spreads
When a check fails, the base must change. Which end? The heel and the toe do different jobs, and a metre of one is not worth a metre of the other.
The heel holds. Every metre of heel carries a column of backfill: 19 × 4.5 = 85.5 kN in the notes’ wall, against 10 kN for the metre of base slab under it. That weight is what the friction and most of the restoring moment come from. If the wall slides, lengthen the heel.
The toe spreads. A longer toe adds almost no weight, but it moves the edge A forward: the resultant then meets the base nearer its centre, the eccentricity falls, and so does the toe pressure. If the toe pressure is too high or the resultant leaves the middle third, lengthen the toe.
[Figure: The same 3.2 m base with the stem moved along it. Sliding wants a long heel; the toe pressure wants a long toe; both pass in between.]
The two jobs pull against each other on a base of fixed width: moving the stem forward lengthens the heel and shortens the toe. For the notes’ 3.2 m base both the sliding check and the toe pressure pass with the toe between 0.32 and 0.66 m. The notes’ 0.8 m toe lies just outside: the wall slides in Combination 2. A toe of 0.6 m with a heel of 2.2 m passes every check with no more concrete than the wall that failed; lengthening the heel alone (base 3.4 m, Worked Example 13.1) passes with 3 % more.
The design loop 1. First dimensions from §1. 2. Pressures and thrusts over H (§2). 3. The table of loads and moments about the toe (§3). 4. Overturning; sliding in combination 1 and in EC7 Combination 2 (§4). 5. The resultant, the middle third and the bearing pressure (§5). 6. If a check fails: the heel for sliding and overturning, the toe for the pressure; then repeat from step 3, since only the weights and their arms change. The thrusts change only if H changes.
Stability sizes the base; it does not design the concrete. A thin base may pass every check here and still fail in bending or shear at the stem. Unit 14 designs the stem, the toe and the heel as cantilevers, with their bars and their detailing, and adds the key, the sloping backfill and the water table.
Quick check (not graded): A wall passes overturning and bearing but fails sliding by 5 %. The change that gains the most friction for the least concrete is
Options: a thicker base | a longer toe | a longer heel | a thicker stem
Explanation shown after answering: A longer heel carries more backfill: 85.5 kN of soil for every 10 kN of concrete in the notes’ wall. A longer toe adds only its own concrete. A thicker base adds a little weight but also raises H, so the thrust grows faster than the friction.
Key points:
- The heel holds: its soil gives the weight, so the friction and the restoring moment.
- The toe spreads: it centres the resultant and lowers the toe pressure.
- On a fixed base the two trade against each other; look for the window where both pass.
- After a change, repeat from the table of loads; the thrusts stay unless H changes.

[examples-x3] Example 3 · Explain-type questions
Exam type short written answers Time ≈ 3 min each
Questions
- For the stability checks, why is the thrust taken over H = 4.9 m and not over the 4.5 m of the stem?
- In a column design the permanent load takes 1.35. Why does the weight of the wall and of the soil take 0.9 against overturning and 1.0 against sliding?
- How can the same wall pass sliding in combination 1 and fail it in EC7 Combination 2?
- A wall passes sliding, but its toe pressure exceeds q_a. Which end of the base would you lengthen, and why?
Write your four answers first, then open the model answers one by one.
## Answer 1 The virtual back
For stability the wall and the block of soil on its heel act as one body, and the back of that body is the vertical plane through the end of the heel: the virtual back. The thrust acts on that plane over its whole height, from the surface to the underside of the base, 4.9 m; the base slab is part of the body being pushed. Taking 4.5 m gives a soil thrust of 52.1 kN instead of 61.8 kN, 16 % too small and on the unsafe side. The 4.5 m is the right height for a different question, the bending of the stem itself (Unit 14).
## Answer 2 Favourable and unfavourable
A partial factor is put where it makes the check harder to pass. In a column the load is what must be resisted, so it takes 1.35. In a stability check the weight is what resists: overstating it would be unsafe, so it takes 0.9 against overturning (EQU) and 1.0 against sliding, while the thrust, which harms, takes 1.1 or 1.35. The surcharge shows the rule most clearly: its thrust takes 1.5 and its weight on the heel takes 0. With 1.35 on the weights the friction of the notes’ wall would read 161.3 kN instead of 119.5 kN.
## Answer 3 The strength of the soil is factored
Combination 1 factors the actions and keeps the soil at its characteristic strength. Combination 2 keeps the actions near their characteristic values (1.0 and 1.3) and divides tan φ and μ by 1.25. For φ = 35°, K_a rises from 0.271 to 0.343: a factor of 1.267 on every thrust, nearly the 1.35 it replaces, so the sliding force hardly changes (103.4 against 100.2 kN). The friction, though, falls by a fifth, from 119.5 to 95.6 kN. For sliding on a frictional base, Combination 2 is close to combination 1 with a fifth of the friction removed, so it governs.
## Answer 4 The toe
The toe. In Faded Example 13.2 the first trial passes sliding (85.4 ≤ 90.0 kN) but its toe pressure is 128.5 > 120 kN/m². Adding 0.5 m to the toe moves the edge A forward: the resultant meets the base 0.061 m from the centre instead of 0.281 m, and the toe pressure falls to 77.3 kN/m² for only 5 kN more load. The same 0.5 m added to the heel brings 46 kN more load, and the toe pressure only falls to 112.2 kN/m². The heel buys friction; the toe buys an even pressure.

[glossary-active-pressure] Glossary: active pressure
active pressure: The smallest sideways pressure of a soil, reached when the wall yields a little away from it: p = K_a (γz + w).

[glossary-allowable-bearing-pressure-q-a] Glossary: allowable bearing pressure, q_a
allowable bearing pressure, q_a: The pressure the ground may carry under service loads; the largest pressure under the base, at the toe, is compared with it.

[glossary-angle-of-shearing-resistance] Glossary: angle of shearing resistance, φ
angle of shearing resistance, φ: The friction angle of the soil; with c = 0 it alone fixes K_a . EC7 Combination 2 uses φ_d = tan⁻¹(tan φ/1.25).

[glossary-backfill] Glossary: backfill
backfill: The soil placed behind the wall after it is built; granular and drained in this course.

[glossary-base] Glossary: base
base: The slab under a cantilever wall: the toe in front of the stem and the heel behind it; width B, thickness h.

[glossary-bearing-pressure] Glossary: bearing pressure
bearing pressure: The pressure between the base and the ground: q = N/B ± 6Ne/B² with service loads, largest at the toe.

[glossary-buttress-wall] Glossary: buttress wall
buttress wall: A wall whose stem is braced by walls in front of it, in compression.

[glossary-cantilever-wall] Glossary: cantilever wall
cantilever wall: A stem fixed to a base slab; it stands mainly by the weight of the backfill on its heel. Economical to about 8 m.

[glossary-coefficient-of-friction] Glossary: coefficient of friction, μ
coefficient of friction, μ: μ = tan δ between the base and the ground; the sliding resistance is μ times the vertical load. Divided by 1.25 in EC7 Combination 2.

[glossary-combination-1] Glossary: combination 1
combination 1: The load-factor combination of the stability checks: thrusts × 1.35 and 1.5, weights × 1.0, soil at its characteristic strength.

[glossary-combination-2-ec7-da1] Glossary: Combination 2 (EC7 DA1)
Combination 2 (EC7 DA1): The second combination of MS EN 1997-1 Design Approach 1: actions × 1.0 and 1.3, tan φ and μ divided by 1.25. It often governs sliding.

[glossary-counterfort-wall] Glossary: counterfort wall
counterfort wall: A wall whose stem and base are tied together by bracing walls behind the stem, in tension; for heights above 6 to 7 m.

[glossary-eccentricity-e] Glossary: eccentricity, e
eccentricity, e: The distance of the resultant from the centre of the base: e = B/2 − x , with x measured from the toe.

[glossary-equ] Glossary: EQU
EQU: The limit state of static equilibrium, used for overturning: 1.1 and 1.5 on what overturns, 0.9 on what restores.

[glossary-favourable-action] Glossary: favourable action
favourable action: A load that helps the check being made. A favourable permanent action takes 0.9 or 1.0; a favourable variable action counts as zero.

[glossary-gravity-wall] Glossary: gravity wall
gravity wall: A wall of plain concrete or masonry that stands by its own weight, with the thrust line kept in the middle third; for low walls.

[glossary-heel] Glossary: heel
heel: The part of the base behind the stem. The backfill stands on it: its weight gives the friction and most of the restoring moment.

[glossary-k-a] Glossary: K_a
K_a: Rankine’s coefficient of active pressure for a level granular backfill: (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ); 0.271 for φ = 35°.

[glossary-lever-arm] Glossary: lever arm
lever arm: The distance of a load from the toe A: horizontal for a weight, vertical (H/3 or H/2 above the underside) for a thrust.

[glossary-middle-third] Glossary: middle third
middle third: The central third of the base. With the resultant inside it (e ≤ B/6) the whole base stays in contact with the ground.

[glossary-overturning] Glossary: overturning
overturning: Rotation of the wall about its toe; checked with moments about A: 1.1M_{o,G} + 1.5M_{o,Q} ≤ 0.9M_{r,G} .

[glossary-passive-resistance] Glossary: passive resistance
passive resistance: The resistance of the soil in front of the base when the wall pushes into it. Ignored in the course checks; used for a key under the base in Unit 14.

[glossary-restoring-moment] Glossary: restoring moment
restoring moment: The moment of a weight about the toe, which turns the wall back onto its heel.

[glossary-resultant] Glossary: resultant
resultant: The single force equal to all the loads on the wall; it meets the base at x = ΔM/N from the toe.

[glossary-sliding] Glossary: sliding
sliding: Movement of the wall forward on its base; resisted by friction, μ times the permanent vertical load.

[glossary-stem] Glossary: stem
stem: The vertical cantilever that holds the soil; about 80 mm thick at its root for every metre of backfill.

[glossary-surcharge-w] Glossary: surcharge, w
surcharge, w: A uniform load on the backfill. It acts twice: a thrust K_a wH at mid-height (unfavourable) and a weight on the heel (favourable, taken as zero in the stability checks).

[glossary-thrust] Glossary: thrust
thrust: The resultant of the active pressure per metre of wall: P_s = ½K_a γH² at H/3 from the soil, P_q = K_a wH at H/2 from the surcharge.

[glossary-toe] Glossary: toe
toe: The part of the base in front of the stem. A longer toe centres the resultant and lowers the toe pressure. Its end, A, is the point the wall would turn about.

[glossary-virtual-back] Glossary: virtual back
virtual back: The vertical plane through the end of the heel, from the surface to the underside of the base (height H); the thrust for stability acts on it.

[glossary-weep-hole] Glossary: weep hole
weep hole: A drain through the stem that keeps water from building up behind the wall.
